#2779. Australia reach World Cup final after Fiji scare

Tries: Church 4, Upton, Chapman Goals: Kelleher 3

Tries: Yaranamua, Paseka Goals: Yaranamua 3

Australia have reached their fifth successive Women's Rugby League World Cup final as they seek a fourth consecutive title - but they were made to work harder than anyone expected.

They had breezed through the group stages and there looked to be little to stop the procession.

But World Cup debutants Fiji had other ideas. For 40 minutes, one of the biggest surprises in the history of rugby league looked eminently possible.

Order was eventually restored, thanks largely to four tries from Abbi Church, which set Australia on their way to a 30-14 victory.

They will face old rivals New Zealand in the final next Sunday in Brisbane, kicking off at 05:10 GMT.

But having given New Zealand a scare in their opening match before losing 18-12, Fiji came out at Sydney Football Stadium fully intent to unsettle and confront the red-hot tournament favourites.

In doing so, they became the first side since New Zealand in the 2013 World Cup final to open the scoring in a game against Australia, who trailed for the first time at this tournament.

"They're the games you want to play," Australia captain Isabelle Kelly said.

"When you have those close games, it shows the character within the girls that are out there and in the battles. For me it was great to see everyone go back out there in the second half and stand up and do what we needed to do.

"You have got to give full respect to the Fijians, they were incredible. We've been watching them closely over the World Cup and supporting them along the way.

"What they've been able to do to come together to create such a special occasion for them, but also what they showcased out of the field was very good, very physical. They were amazing."

Church scores four as Australia beat Fiji to reach Women's RL World Cup final - as it happened

The tournament debutants put pressure on the Australia line from the start. Soon the entire Aussie team caught the bug with simple drops and brainless errors, and after 12 minutes Simaima Taufa conceded a penalty under the posts.

Fiji opted to kick for two points. Four minutes later, they went all the way.

Captain Sereana Naitokatoka stole the ball from Jaime Chapman 10 metres from the Australia line, and they drove through the defence for half-back Luisa Yaranamua to score. She also converted to give Fiji an astonishing 8-0 lead.

At last Australia sparked into life, and two tries in the final 10 minutes of the opening half brought them level.

Church drove over in the right corner, before Tamika Upton slipped through the defence as Australia returned pressure following a Fiji drop-out.

But Jocelyn Kelleher missed twice from the tee to allow Fiji in at half-time level. Had Upton not brilliantly tipped a Fiji grubber behind, Australia would have trailed.

Whatever coach Jess Skinner said in the changing room woke Australia up, and they took control.

Church completed her treble - the third a brilliant catch from a booming Tarryn Aiken kick to the corner and before grounding the ball at full tilt - either side of Chapman diving over.

Normal service resumed. But at last, the Jillaroos have been proved fallible - with a late Maria Paseka try providing a deserved flourish for fearless Fiji.

"I'm so happy," Naitokatoka said afterwards. "What a game.

"It was so exciting. We just had fun, not thinking too much. Just run hard, play hard, that was our goal. Everyone came out of there happy knowing they've put their best throughout the whole 70 minutes."

Church, though, had the last word for Australia - collecting Losana Lutu's kick around 30 metres from her own line before racing clear to score.

"I have so much respect for Abbi," said Kelly. "All year round she's incredible. Everyone thinks she's a full-back but she could play anywhere and dominate a role.

"Abbi is the ultimate team-mate. She's a quiet one but she gets about her work to make sure she can perform her best. As a team-mate I've been so proud of her the past two years."

Abbi Church scored twice against England and two more against Wales in the pool stage [Getty Images]

There was a point in this game where Fiji had the Jillaroos sweating somewhat and Abbi Church came up with an outstanding piece of individual skill to break the Buli Kula with a dance infield and score.

It was a significant moment within a side packed with talent that swung the favour back toward Australia and it was just one of several major touches in the contest.

She tracked a delightful Tarryn Aiken kick to score one of her four tries, in addition to busting Fiji with four line breaks, six tackle breaks and 205 metres accrued.

The energy of Keeley Nizza from dummy half was crucial, Olivia Kernick's industry and the class of Isabelle Kelly and Tamika Upton all contributed to the win, while Fiji's Luisa Yaranamua and Cassie Staples stood up, but Church was the leading light for me.

#2778. Report: Colts are in trade talks regarding QB Daniel Jones

The Indianapolis fire sale could indeed extend to the man who was supposed to become a franchise quarterback there.

According to ESPNFL, the Colts have engaged in trade talks this week regarding Daniel Jones, speaking to “multiple teams.”

The precise language of the report identifies only one team as actually talking to the Colts. From the article, the Ravens “were one team to check in on Jones.” The Ravens ultimately struck a deal with the Cardinals for quarterback Jacoby Brissett, whose plunge from No. 1 to No. 3 on the depth chart made it clear to the rest of the league that he was available.

The only other team mentioned by name is the Vikings, and the report points only to "[s]peculation” involving Minnesota. (We’ve been “speculating” about it since the immediate aftermath of Sunday’s loss by the Vikings in Detroit.)

Past ESPNFL reporting on a potential trade for running back Jonathan Taylor ultimately listed five teams as talking to the Colts (Giants, Seahawks, Broncos, Packers, Vikings). The fact that other teams weren’t mentioned as to Jones suggests that, frankly, there may not be other teams.

Really, which current contender would want him? The Vikings are the only potential playoff team that checks the box as possibly needing a starter right now. And only the Vikings and Giants are contenders with which Jones has direct experience. (The Giants wouldn’t want a Jones reunion, and Jones surely wouldn’t want it, either.)

That could change this weekend, obviously. One injury to a starter could alter the dynamics, spurring another contender to pick up the phone and make a push for Jones. The most memorable example of that came 15 years ago, when a broken collarbone to Raiders quarterback Jason Campbell prompted a quick deal for Bengals quarterback Carson Palmer, who had decided he didn’t want to play for the team that had drafted him — and who had yet to report.

Three years ago, Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins popped an Achilles tendon two days before the deadline, forcing the Vikings to scramble at the deadline to do a deal with the Cardinals for quarterback Josh Dobbs.

Absent a multi-week injury to a starting quarterback on a contender that doesn’t believe its backup can hold down the fort, the Vikings may be the only team that wants Jones at the deadline.

The preferences of Daniel Jones become a factor, too. If (as we firmly believe) he’s not happy that the Colts folded the tents by trading guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner after a 2-5 start that included an overtime loss to the Chiefs and a toe-to-toe battle with the then-unbeaten Vikings, Jones would have a clear interest in hopping to a contender.

The Vikings wanted to keep Jones after the 2024 season. He opted to sign with the Colts in part because he saw a more realistic path to winning the job over 2023 first-rounder Anthony Richardson in Indianapolis than 2024 first-rounder J.J. McCarthy in Minneapolis. If he’s told that a return to Minnesota would include being installed immediately as QB1, he’d surely prefer that to a lost season with the Colts.

Andd Jones has power over this process. Beyond the basic reality that no team wants a starting quarterback who doesn’t want to play for it, the 2027 roster bonus and base salary that become fully guaranteed in March ($10.51 million) are currently guaranteed for injury. The ESPNFL article mentions that Jones could waive the injury guarantee in order to expedite a deal.

The reverse of that (Jones refusing to waive the injury guarantee) means that Jones could block a trade, if avoiding a potential eight-figure guarantee for 2027 is a dealbreaker for his prospective employer.

Our guess? Right now, only the Vikings currently have interest in Jones. And a trade for Jones becomes a very viable possibility if the Vikings lose to the Bills on Monday with Carson Wentz playing quarterback.

Given the possibility that another team will emerge as a competitor to get Jones, it’s also possible that the Vikings have already decided to trade for Jones after Monday night’s game — win or lose — and that the two teams have agreed to keep it under wraps until Week 9 ends.

Either way, if the oft-injured Jones plays on Sunday against the Cowboys and gets injured, that would kill any chance to trade him. That makes it important to monitor Sunday’s game carefully. If the Colts apply a quick hook to Jones, it could mean that he’s already gone.

#2775. Cleveland Browns news: It is going to be a day, that’s for sure!

Today's slate of games opens early as the Cincinnati Bengals and Atlanta Falcons tangle in Madrid, Spain, at 9:30 a.m.

The day closes with Tampa Bay taking on Chicago in a renewal of an old NFC Central clash on Sunday Night Football.

And in between? Oh, nothing much, just what will be the most over-analyzed Cleveland Browns game of the season as they face the New Orleans Saints.

If the Browns are serious about staying in the playoff race, there is no excuse to lose this game. The Saints are bad and have nothing to play for. Cleveland's defense should be good enough to limit whatever New Orleans wants to do on offense.

But all the attention will be on Cleveland's offense, as Shedeur Sanders is making a spot start at quarterback while Deshaun Watson is still in the concussion protocol.

There is already talk that if Sanders looks even remotely competent, head coach Todd Monken will bench Watson and turn Cleveland's playoff hopes over to Sanders in an attempt to "see what the Browns have." Never mind that Monken has never once even hinted that he would consider such lunacy.

Watson has not been playing good, but in Cleveland's wins he has been good enough. And there is no evidence to support the idea that the Browns would be in the playoff picture in November if Sanders had been the starter from Week 1.

It's the Browns and quarterbacks, so people tend to get irrational. But there isn't a single team in the league that would bench its starter and go with a backup in this situation, so there is no reason for the Browns to be trendsetters.

Sanders gets the start today, because that is what the backup quarterback does when the starter is out. Then, as soon as the starter is cleared to play, things go back to the way they were.

The Browns need to win this game, and it doesn't matter how they do it as long as they accomplish that goal. But no matter what happens, the quarterback pecking order is established and is not changing.

#2773. Player Personnel Handbook implies that the NFL can delay (or deny) Brandon Aiyuk's reinstatement

Until very recently, people throughout the league believed that the procedure for returning from the reserve/left squad list was administrative, and essentially automatic.

The Brandon Aiyuk case shows that, in the NFL’s view, it definitely is not.

The Collective Bargaining Agreement is silent on the topic of the reserve/left squad list. The relevant language regarding placement (and eventual reinstatement) from the reserve/left squad list appears in the NFL’s Player Personnel Handbook.

In the year when the player is placed on reserve/left squad, he can’t play for his current team or any other team. His season is basically over. The window for reinstatement opens the next year.

Here’s the key language from the Player Personnel Handbook regarding reinstatement: “A player on Reserve/Left Squad must apply to the Commissioner for reinstatement to his club’s Active List. No player on Reserve/Left Squad shall be reinstated in the same season in which he is placed on Reserve. A player applying for reinstatement in a season subsequent to the season in which he is placed on Reserve/Left Squad is prohibited from being reinstated in the last 30 days of the regular season or thereafter during the postseason, and no such player will be reinstated during the period between the trading deadline of a subsequent season and the 30-day deadline unless the club initiates the reinstatement request and the Commissioner approves it.”

While the provision doesn’t say it expressly, the language implies that the Commissioner has apparently unlimited discretion when it comes to approving the application to reinstate the player. In Aiyuk’s case, the Commissioner has dragged his feet since October 27, setting the stage for an apparent effort by the 49ers to leverage Aiyuk’s desire to be reinstated to his willingness to reimburse up to $13 million in previously-paid bonus money.

The NFL Players Association has remained silent throughout the process, and perhaps for good reason. The absence of any provision in the CBA regarding the mechanics of the reserve/left squad list arguably means that the situation falls within the NFL’s “management rights” clause, which allows the various teams “to manage and direct their operations in any manner whatsoever, except as specifically limited by the provisions of this Agreement.”

With no limitations in the CBA as to the operation of the reserve/left squad list (or reinstatement from it), the NFLPA may be without options.

Precedent becomes relevant to the overall analysis. How has the league handled past requests for reinstatement from the reserve/left squad list? If the league has previously not delayed reinstatement (for whatever reason), there’s an argument to be made that it should not be delayed as to Aiyuk.

Regardless, it’s becoming increasingly obvious that the NFL and the 49ers are working together to tie Aiyuk’s reinstatement to his satisfaction of the debt that the 49ers believe Aiyuk has incurred through his prior default under his contract. It should be two separate issues, with the 49ers having the ability to pursue the recovery of bonus money from Aiyuk and Aiyuk having the ability to be reinstated. By tying the two together, the 49ers have found a way to condition Aiyuk’s reinstatement on his willingness to wire a significant payment to the 49ers.

Can the NFL and the 49ers do that? For now, they are. The question is whether Aiyuk and/or the NFLPA can come up with a legal argument against the obvious effort to block Aiyuk’s return until he returns millions to the 49ers.

If Aiyuk wants to be reinstated quickly, his best (and perhaps only) play will be to return millions to the 49ers, with the ensuing goal of earning it back as his career continues elsewhere.

#2772. Cam Jordan will become third defensive player to play 250 games with same team

When the Saints host the Browns on Sunday, New Orleans defensive end Cam Jordan will reach a rare milestone.

The Week 9 game will be Jordan’s 250th. Via NBC Sports research, Jordan will become only the third defensive player in NFL history to play 250 or more games with the same team.

The others are Darrell Green, who played 295 games for Washington from 1983 through 2002, and Jim Marshall, who played 270 games for the Vikings from 1961 through 1979.

Jordan, the son of former Vikings tight end Steve Jordan, was a first-round pick in 2011. His dad played in 176 games from 1982 through 1994.

Cam is an eight-time Pro Bowler, with 132.0 career sacks. He’s currently 22nd on the all-time list.

#2768. Nets at Mavericks Preview

The Mavericks finally got back on track Friday night with a 112-100 win over the Utah Jazz, and now they get another very winnable game Sunday against the Brooklyn Nets. Dallas enters at 5-4 after snapping a two-game losing streak, while Brooklyn entered the weekend at 2-6 and has to come to Dallas on the second night of a back-to-back after playing Atlanta on Saturday.

This is the type of game Dallas needs to start taking care of consistently. The Mavericks have already shown they can hang with much better teams, but losses like the one to Sacramento have also shown how quickly things can go sideways when they play down to an opponent. Brooklyn has enough legitimate NBA talent to make that happen again if Dallas comes out flat.

The Jazz win wasn't perfect, but there were plenty of encouraging signs.

Cooper Flagg finished with 21 points, 10 rebounds, and seven assists despite another slow start; P.J. Washington carried the offense early with 26 points, and Morez Johnson Jr. was fantastic with 13 points and 17 rebounds, including 10 on the offensive glass. Santi Aldama also made his season debut, giving Dallas eight points and nine rebounds in just 13 minutes.

That is the kind of collective production Dallas needs. Kyrie Irving and Flagg combined to shoot just 3-of-17 in the first half against Utah, but the Mavericks survived until both eventually got going. Dallas has spent too much of the early season needing Flagg or Kyrie to solve everything. Friday was a good example of what this roster can look like when Washington, Morez and the rest of the rotation actually give them something.

Brooklyn should give Dallas another opportunity to build on that.

Morez Johnson Jr. might be forcing Dusty May's hand.

The rookie was one of Dallas' best players Friday, dominating the offensive glass and giving the Mavericks the type of physicality they have badly needed with Dereck Lively II still sidelined. His 17-rebound performance was easily one of the biggest reasons Dallas controlled the second half against Utah.

Brooklyn has size with Julius Randle, Michael Porter Jr., Day'Ron Sharpe and Noah Clowney, so this will not be an easy matchup on the glass. But Morez has earned another real opportunity. Dallas has struggled with rebounding far too often this season, and right now the rookie is giving May something that is hard to take off the floor.

Aldama's return only makes the frontcourt rotation more interesting.

The Nets are young, but their two best players are not.

Michael Porter Jr. entered the weekend averaging 21.4 points and 7.4 rebounds, while Julius Randle was averaging 21 points, 7.1 rebounds, and 4.8 assists. Porter is still one of the league's more dangerous shooters when he gets comfortable, and Randle can punish smaller defenders if Dallas lets him establish position and work downhill.

That should make Washington especially important again. Dallas needs someone who can handle Randle physically without constantly forcing help, while the rest of the defense stays attached to Porter.

The Nets aren't good enough for Dallas to treat this like some impossible matchup, but they have enough individual scoring talent to make the Mavericks pay for another lazy defensive night.

This is really what Sunday comes down to.

Dallas just started a three-game homestand with a win over Utah and gets Brooklyn before Indiana comes to town Monday. The Mavericks do not need anything spectacular here. They need to defend, rebound and avoid spending the first half trying to wake themselves up.

Brooklyn will also be playing its second game in as many nights, while Dallas has Saturday off. The Mavericks have no reason to be the team lacking energy.

Dallas has already played enough difficult games to start the season. Against teams like Brooklyn, the goal should be simple: don't make the game harder than it needs to be.

When: Sunday, November 8, 6:30 p.m. CTWhere: American Airlines Center, Dallas, Texas

As of Saturday evening, Dereck Lively II, Sergio de Larrea and Tarik Biberovic are listed out for Dallas, while Caleb Martin is available. Brooklyn had not yet submitted its official injury report for Sunday's game at the time of the latest NBA report.

#2767. Deion Sanders says Colorado deserves better after falling to 3-6

Colorado lost again on Saturday night, and afterward head coach Deion Sanders said he knows his team isn’t good enough.

Saturday’s 20-10 loss to Arizona State dropped Colorado to 3-6 this season, and dropped Sanders to 19-27 in four years as Colorado’s head coach.

“The season doesn’t look good,” Sanders said afterward. “It doesn’t look good. I’m not crazy. I can see clearly. You think I’m happy? I’m not happy with the outcomes. I’m not a loser by any means, and I hate the fact that we’re coming up on the short end of these games.”

Sanders ran through the stats from the game and then said his team hadn’t played well enough.

“The fan base deserves better. They really do,” Sanders said.

Ultimately, Sanders says, it’s on him to coach better.

“We’ve just got to do better,” Sanders said. “And that starts with me.”

#2764. Hall of Fame LB Jack Ham hospitalized after medical emergency at Penn State game

Hall of Fame linebacker Jack Ham, who now serves as a radio analyst for Penn State football, was hospitalized in Seattle on Saturday after experiencing a medical emergency.

Penn State coach Matt Campbell said after the 28-25 win over Washington that Ham was assisted by play-by-play announcer Steve Jones.

“If it’s not for Steve, what he did, I don’t know if we have as good a news as we do right now,” Campbell said, via Adam Rittenberg of ESPN. Campbell added that Jones’s efforts to save Ham were “heroic.”

#2762. Stephen Curry drops 41 points vs. Magic as Warriors win seventh straight in OT

The Golden State Warriors began their season with the first 0-3 start of Stephen Curry's career. They are now 7-3.

Curry led the Warriors to their seventh straight win on Saturday, dropping 41 points to beat the Orlando Magic 126-119 in overtime. Golden State now sits in a tie for fifth in a competitive Western Conference.

In addition to his 41 points, Curry posted 6 rebounds and 6 assists while shooting 13-of-19 from the field (5-of-10 from 3-point range). Several of those points came at an inconvenient time for Orlando.

With a 10-for-10 performance at the free throw line, Curry is also now 66-of-67 from the charity stripe in eight games this season.

In addition to Curry, Yaxel Lendeborg continued a strong rookie season with 23 points, 8 rebounds, 3 assists, 3 blocks and 6 turnovers.

The game began as a one-sided affair for the Warriors, who led by 16 at halftime only for a third-quarter run to give the Magic the lead. The rest of the game was close, with Orlando forward Jamal Cain making a putback lay-up to tie the game with two seconds left.

Curry and Lendeborg combined to score the Warriors' final 12 points to put the game away in overtime.

It was easy to feel like the Warriors were in a bad place for the long term at the start of the season. Jimmy Butler is likely out until January. It's unclear when Kristaps Porzingis will play basketball again. Moses Moody is also weeks away from a return.

Golden State was, and still is, an unquestionably old team committed to winning now with Curry, but got bounced in the playoffs last year and had the NBA world wondering if this was the summer they would blow it all up. They didn't, and then they posted their worst three-game start since drafting Curry.

You don't need to remind the Warriors of where the vibes were then, as Curry mentioned after Saturday's game:

"We don't forget where people thought we were at the beginning of the year."

That team now has the second-longest winning streak in the NBA, behind only the San Antonio Spurs' eight straight victories. Next up is a home game against the New Orleans Pelicans on Monday.

#2759. Preview: Surviving a pack of Wolves

We won't deny it: the last week or so has consisted of games that have been a 'must-win' for Utah. And tonight is included.

The team's play against Dallas was more on the promising side: fans saw Darryn Peterson start to find his groove and play like the #2 pick he is, Lauri Markkanen hit a mind-boggling eight triples, but it feels like Utah needs to play a perfect and synchronised game of basketball just to win a game of basketball.

The Jazz road trip concludes with a visit to see our divisional foe, along with former friends in Minnesota. The roster overhaul over the 2026 offseason added star LaMelo Ball to the mix, designed to alleviate the facilitating role for Anthony Edwards. They've even got a brand-spankin' new rebrand as the league adapts to the dying trend of minimalism. The Wolves are so unrecognisable that they even have Rudy Gobert looking like Montel Williams.

The addition of LaMelo and Kuminga has given them an early season boost. They hold a +5.1 rebound-per-game improvement compared to the baseline average of 49.2 rebounds per game last season. They've also maintained their defensive core to post a 106.6 defensive rating, second-best in the Association. After a hot 3-0 start, the Wolves have sizzled to a comfortable 7-3 record to sit at the 6th spot in the Western Conference.

Minnesota's rebounding is arguably Utah's biggest concern if they're chasing a win. They rank 2nd in the NBA in offensive rebound percentage (35.6%), making them a formidable foe for a team already missing Jusuf Nurkic. The team needs to stay disciplined, ensuring that every player sticks to boxing out.

It's especially important that the Jazz shooting woes need to be put on hold, or else they'll get punished on the other end. They have converted just 28% of their three-point attempts over the last three games (34-of-121). While they demonstrated minor improvement against Dallas, the overall efficiency continues to be a lingering issue. Missed shots could quickly translate into transition opportunities for the Wolves, while their offensive rebounding allows them to compensate for their own missed attempts.

And really, I don't know if it's possible to hold your own if Mo Bamba is another healthy scratch from the rotation, with a DNP-CD against Dallas, in favour of Tony Bradley. Perhaps his ankle flared up before tonight, but either way, Utah needs some size advantage.

NEW ORLEANS, LA – NOVEMBER 4: Jaxson Hayes #11 of the Utah Jazz goes up for the rebound during the game against the New Orleans Pelicans on November 4, 2026 at the Smoothie King Center in New Orleans, Louisiana. It feels like it's been years since the Jazz were a bottom-10 team in turnovers. The lack of winning experience, combined with inconsistent offensive flow, has left the Jazz with a 17.2% turnover rate, ranking them 26th in the league.

This was evident when the Jazz coughed up 21 turnovers in their NBA Cup loss to the Mavericks. Will Hardy specifically highlighted the team's concerns about handling the ball and maintaining an offensive flow:

The ball movement that was promised still hasn't come to fruition. Things seem stagnant, relying heavily on Keyonte and Lauri to create their own shots rather than having them come to them naturally. Yes, a large part of it is them missing their distributing big man, Nurkic (whom will likely miss the rest of November), but it seems like they're trying to force-feed their top guys more than anything else.

Minnesota already rank eighth in opponent turnover percentage (16.04%), with McDaniels and Kuminga pressuring opposing teams on the perimeter. The Jazz can't lose focus. They will need to become more decisive, make quicker reads, and avoid unnecessary dribbling or else they risk the Timberwolves running away with this one.

The serious advantage in Utah's deck of cards is Minnesota's absence of Anthony Edwards for the next couple of months. When the Wolves win, it comes from contributions from several players rather than relying on a dominant scorer. Utah should look to disrupt the Timberwolves' flow by forcing their second and third options into difficult situations and preventing them from getting comfortable in the early going.

Utah's job tonight will be limiting the role of All-Star LaMelo Ball along with Minnesota's array of perimeter shooters, including Terrence Shannon Jr. and Bones Hyland. Dosunmu exploded for 26 points in New Orleans a couple days ago, so he'll be expected to carry that momentum into tonight.

It's also important to highlight the progression of Jaden McDaniels, posting a career-high 17.1 points per game and a 51.1% field-goal percentage if the season ended today. McDaniels also ranks first with the best offensive rating in the fourth quarter (141.3).

There's little room for error if the Jazz hope to beat a proven Playoff team. It feels like this has been the story for weeks, but seriously, it's do-or-die time for the Jazz to save this season.

#2756. San Antonio vs. Portland, Final Score: Spurs dispatch Trail Blazers, improve to 2-0 on road trip, 125-103

Both sides were on the second night of a back-to-back set, and the San Antonio Spurs handled the Portland Trail Blazers on the road. This was the first matchup between last year's first-round opponent and it was uncommonly physical for a November game.

The Spurs didn't shoot well early, but were the nastier team from tip-off, getting into the bonus in fewer than six minutes and forcing a few turnovers. Their quickness shifting into the lane tempted the Blazers into too many unsuccessful 3-point attempts which sparked transition, but they got sloppy, committing too many fouls and that bad habit persisted most of the first half.

The Trail Blazers stayed on their heels with relentless hustle, and then the Silver and Black cracked the code. Eventually, Victor Wembanyama also went on a tear that zapped whatever will the hosts had left. He had 29 points, seven rebounds and three assists. His biggest help came from Stephon Castle, who played a nice all-around game with 14 points, seven rebounds and five assists, plus Devin Vassell, who added 15 points and two steals.

Garbage time started when they built up a 32-point lead late in the third quarter.

The Trail Blazers were down one penetrator in Ja Morant, which affected their ability to bend the defense. On top of that, the schemes made Portland look ordinary at their downhill game and they never countered with feeding Donovan Clingan in the post. Their rebounding helped keep them in the game but that only lasted for so long.

The Spurs played with high intensity but in the first half, not much discipline. All those cheap fouls had three of them in foul trouble and prevented them from continuing their work in transition, giving the Blazers an opportunity to start creeping in through the door.

The Trail Blazers are a long, athletic team with good screen navigation, so getting by them into the lane can be a challenge. The Spurs' jump-shooting unfastened their defense, but they started playing more forcefully on the perimeter and made it tougher to maneuver. The Spurs were not phased and kept plugging away, shooting 77.3 percent in the restricted area.

It seems that Castle brings it when is playing his old teammate, Clingan. He was one of the team's best rebounders, and he was like a linebacker stopping the run game inside, especially from Deni Avdija.

It was a rough shooting night before the game broke open, and the team got a big lift from Julian Champagnie, making four 3-pointers, including two consecutive treys in the second quarter, when the team badly needed it.

Toumani Camara said the plan was to get physical with Wembanyama before the game, and they did, not giving him much room after catches, bumping him on the move and using some hand checks. This played a big part in him going eight-for-nine at the line. The extra stuff did not wear him down physically or mentally.

Exhibit A. of the game flipping like a light switch: the Spurs made 17 first-half field goals had 18 in the third quarter.

The Spurs eventually took an edge on the glass 13 and added 23 back-breaking second-chance points.

Carter Bryant got subbed into the game early in the second quarter, and his minutes were mostly negative because his aggressiveness can be used against him. He had three fouls in three minutes, yet coach Mitch Johnson gave him a chance to make up for it with extra time and later as well when the game was out of reach.

#2754. Player Grades: Cavs vs Knicks – Donovan Mitchell drops 37 points in loss

The Cleveland Cavaliers fell 109-97 to the New York Knicks on the second night of a back-to-back.

Grades are based on our usual expectations for each player.

Mitchell looks like he's finding the right balance between scoring and passing through the last two games. He's been aggressive first, allowing his playmaking to come as a result of the defense overreacting to his gravity. That's led to some efficient games passing the ball, but we were all waiting for Mitchell to have a scorching hot game shooting it.

Mitchell went off for a season-high 37 points, and he was the catalyst behind Cleveland's momentary comeback in the fourth quarter. Mitchell was one of the only Cavaliers who had a pulse on offense tonight.

12 points, 9 rebounds, 5 assists, 3 turnovers

Mobley was fantastic last night against the Philadelphia 76ers. Tonight? He was totally on his back foot.

Karl-Anthony Towns beat Mobley to the punch more often than not. It was an uber-aggressive approach from KAT that reminded you why the Cavs are still at their best when there are two defensive anchors on the floor.

We know that Mobley can play better than this, and his grade will reflect that.

Last year's playoffs showed that this was a bad matchup for Harden, and tonight proved that it wasn't just because Harden was gassed. The Knicks are too fast and incorporate too much off-ball movement for Harden to keep up defensively. The Cavs will be in trouble if they draw New York again in April or May.

The Cavs have leaned heavily on this 20-year-old rookie to give them minutes. He's had moments where it all clicks effortlessly into place. And other times, he looks off Mitchell and attempts a wild layup that goes the other way in transition.

Thomas shot 3-10 from the floor and looked like a rookie tonight. Overall, he has been fantastic given the circumstances. He's quickly lapped his competition as the best backup guard option on Cleveland's roster. But moments like this are inevitable.

The Cavs need Watson to start shooting the rock better than he has. Watson was 1-of-5 from downtown tonight, and the Knicks had no interest in defending him. For all the potential benefits Watson can bring to this team — it will all feel moot if he can't provide enough spacing to make defenses care about him.

There can be a trickle-down effect in games where the stars struggle to set the tone. Hezonja never found his rhythym in this game, shooting 0-of-6 from the floor. And while he's the only one who can take accountability for that, I think he was more a victim of this team struggling to find its stride as a whole.

I owe Bryant an apology for not grading him last game. It was an honest mistake, and he delivered quality minutes in Cleveland's win over the 76ers.

It brings me no joy to report that he struggled in this matchup. Bryant has become a necessity with Allen on the sidelines, but his lack of mobility made it hard to keep him on the floor.

Proctor has given good minutes during this stretch of poor injury luck for the Cavs. He's showing he's a capable shooter and someone who can occasionally make things happen with the ball in his hands, but he still needs some fine-tuning on both ends of the court to be a player who is in the nightly rotation once everything settles.

The Cavs waived Minix just days ago, before bringing him back only a few hours before tip-off. He responded with the best game of his young career, nailing his first three shots and ending with 8 points.

DeMarvion Overshown's bit hit on Cardinals running back costs him big bucks.

The NFL has issued a fine of $9,528 to Dallas Cowboys linebacker DeMarvion Overshown for the use of his helmet on a hit that knocked Arizona Cardinals running back Bam Knight out of the game last week, per multiple reports. Knight took the hit to the helmet from Overshown in the second quarter, which forced a fumble that the Cowboys recovered. Overshown led with his shoulder and made contact with Knight's head, but the play was not penalized.

#2752. 5 Keys to a New England Patriots Victory Over the Green Bay Packers in Week 9

The New England Patriots have an opportunity to make a statement Sunday afternoon when they host the Green Bay Packers at Gillette Stadium in one of the more intriguing matchups of Week 9.

Both teams enter the game at 5-3, having won four of their last five contests. The Patriots are coming off a 24-19 victory over the Miami Dolphins, while the Packers defeated the Carolina Panthers 27-19.

For Mike Vrabel's Patriots, this represents another opportunity to demonstrate that their resurgence is more than a favorable stretch of scheduling. Green Bay brings a dangerous passing attack led by Jordan Love and a defense capable of creating turnovers and disrupting opposing quarterbacks.

New England has its own difference-maker in Drake Maye, but the third-year quarterback will be operating without two important offensive weapons. Wide receiver A.J. Brown has been ruled out with ankle and knee injuries, while running back TreVeyon Henderson will miss the game because of an illness.

With both teams looking to strengthen their playoff positioning, the outcome could hinge on a handful of critical matchups.

Here are five keys to a Patriots victory over Green Bay.

Maye has demonstrated that he can make the throws necessary to beat quality NFL defenses. The challenge Sunday will be giving him enough time to find opportunities against a Green Bay unit that has been among the league's best.

The Packers enter the game ranked fifth in defensive expected points added per play, according to SumerSports, and their defense has produced 15 takeaways, second-most in the NFL.

There is some encouraging news for New England. Star Green Bay pass rusher Micah Parsons has been ruled out with a knee injury, removing one of the league's most disruptive defensive players from the matchup.

That doesn't mean Maye will have an easy afternoon.

Green Bay defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon can still create pressure through scheme and disguise. The Patriots must identify pressure before the snap, avoid negative plays and give Maye opportunities to challenge the secondary.

With Brown unavailable, New England cannot depend on one receiver consistently winning difficult individual matchups. The passing game will need contributions throughout the receiving corps.

If the offensive line gives Maye time, the Patriots have a chance to create explosive plays against a defense that thrives on forcing mistakes.

One of New England's most important defensive decisions will involve how aggressively to pressure Love.

The Patriots have blitzed on 37.8% of opposing dropbacks this season, the seventh-highest rate in the NFL, according to NBC Sports Boston.

Ordinarily, that aggressiveness can disrupt an offense's timing. Against Love, however, it carries considerable risk.

The Packers quarterback leads the league with 824 passing yards against the blitz, making him particularly dangerous when defenses commit additional rushers.

That creates an interesting tactical challenge for Vrabel and the Patriots' defensive staff.

New England cannot allow Love to stand comfortably in the pocket, but repeatedly sending extra defenders could leave the secondary exposed to quick throws, screens and explosive gains.

The solution may be selective pressure rather than constant pressure.

The Patriots need to disguise their intentions, generate a pass rush with four defenders whenever possible and force Love to hold the football.

Christian Barmore's presence along the defensive front could be especially important, both in collapsing the pocket and disrupting Green Bay's offensive rhythm.

Making Love work through his progressions, rather than giving him obvious blitz opportunities to exploit, could determine whether New England can contain the Packers' passing attack.

Few statistics better illustrate the challenge facing New England than the turnover numbers.

Green Bay has forced 15 turnovers through eight games, while the Patriots have committed 15 giveaways.

That is a dangerous combination for a team facing an opponent capable of capitalizing on short fields.

The encouraging development for New England is Maye's improvement in protecting the football.

After committing seven turnovers in his first three games, Maye has turned it over just three times in his last five appearances.

The Patriots cannot afford unnecessary risks against a defense that has consistently created extra possessions. Maye needs to recognize disguised coverage, protect the ball when pressured and understand when throwing it away is the correct decision.

New England's defense also needs to create opportunities of its own.

Love's willingness to attack downfield gives the Patriots chances to challenge receivers at the catch point and potentially generate interceptions.

In a matchup between two evenly matched teams, one turnover could be the difference between winning and losing.

With Henderson unavailable and Brown sidelined, the Patriots cannot allow their offense to become entirely dependent on Maye making difficult throws.

A productive rushing attack would help New England control possession, limit Green Bay's pass-rush opportunities and create more manageable third downs.

The Packers will be missing linebacker Zaire Franklin, while their offensive opponent also has a chance to benefit from the absence of Parsons.

New England should test Green Bay's defensive front early, even if the initial results are modest.

The objective isn't necessarily to dominate on the ground. It's to make the Packers respect the possibility of a run, particularly on early downs.

That would create opportunities for play-action passes and prevent Green Bay from consistently attacking Maye in obvious passing situations.

The Patriots must also avoid abandoning the run if the Packers build an early lead.

A balanced offensive approach would help compensate for their missing playmakers and keep the game from becoming a contest decided entirely by which quarterback can make the most spectacular throws.

The Packers have relied heavily on Love this season, throwing the football on 66.1% of their offensive plays, the second-highest rate in the NFL.

Their rushing attack has been far less productive.

Green Bay enters Sunday's matchup averaging just 60.6 rushing yards per game, the lowest figure in the league. Even with Josh Jacobs in the backfield, the Packers have struggled to establish consistent production on the ground.

That gives New England a clear defensive objective.

The Patriots must control the line of scrimmage, limit Jacobs on early downs and force Green Bay into predictable passing situations.

Doing so would allow New England to concentrate more resources on coverage and create opportunities for its defensive front to pressure Love without blitzing excessively.

But defensive success alone won't be enough.

The Patriots must turn productive offensive possessions into touchdowns rather than settling for field goals. With both quarterbacks capable of generating explosive plays, red-zone efficiency could become decisive.

That is especially important if windy conditions at Gillette Stadium make longer field-goal attempts more difficult.

New England needs to capitalize when it gets inside the 20-yard line and avoid allowing Green Bay to stay within striking distance.

The Patriots and Packers enter Sunday with identical records and legitimate reasons to believe they can make a playoff run.

Green Bay's passing attack and opportunistic defense present serious challenges, but New England has advantages it can exploit.

Parsons' absence should help Maye, while the Packers' struggling rushing attack gives the Patriots an opportunity to dictate how Green Bay moves the football.

Ultimately, the game could come down to which young quarterback receives the most support.

If New England protects Maye, limits turnovers, stays disciplined against Love and finishes drives, the Patriots have every reason to believe they can emerge with an important home victory.

#2750. Gladbach bosses blame Itakura for “bitter” red card after defeat to Hamburg

Ko Itakura's red card initiated Borussia Mönchengladbach's 3-1 defeat to HSV in the opening game of matchday 9 in Bundesliga. The game was tied 1-1 when the Japanese international saw his second booking only four minutes after the restart.

“If you get a red card shortly after half-time, that's bad,” Gladbach's sporting director Rouven Schröder spoke about the incident in a post-match interview with Sky Sports. “Ko (Itakura) knows that himself. The game was so intense, and you have to finish it with eleven men.

“We talked about it at half-time. It's very tough when you're already on a yellow card. Ko also has a certain amount of experience. He needs to handle things differently,”

Gladbach's coach Alexander Blessin also criticized the player who returned to the club after an unsuccessful spell at Ajax. “The turning point was the yellow-red card. If we had finished the game with eleven men, we definitely would have gotten something out of it. It's obviously bitter," said the coach who replaced Eugen Polanski after Gladbach's poor start to the campaign.

“We gave it our all, but it's just stupid because we ended up with ten men due to such a silly mistake.”

There were similar words by the goalkeeper Daniel Batz and returnee Kevin Diks as they felt the red card was the turning point of the game. #2749. Fans think Florida State hit new low as Boston College use ‘ring around the rosy’ tactic

Even though they got the win against Boston College, one trick play from the Eagles embarrassed the Seminoles.

Florida State managed to beat Boston College 31-24 in their first game without Mike Norvell, who was let go following their loss to Clemson.

After absorbing a $50 million buyout to let Norvell go, fans of the Seminoles needed a big win. And even though the fans got their big win, one play did add another embarrassing moment to a season chock-full of them.

During the third quarter of their game against the Florida State Seminoles, Boston College were at 2nd and Goal when they attempted a unique play.

After a bizarre moving huddle, the Eagles pulled off a trick play with a fake handoff before Mason McKenzie made an underhand pass to Javarius Green for a touchdown.

Understandably, many fans pointed out how bizarre it was to see this trick play, which was made famous by 1974's hit movie, The Longest Yard, starring Burt Reynolds, who was also an alumnus of Florida State.

One fan wrote: "No way the 'ring around the rosy' huddle worked."

However, a Seminoles fan shared a screenshot of the result and mocked Boston College: "Hope the theatre kid antics were worth it."

A third fan pointed out the history of the play in the NFL: "Didn't Andy Reid do the same thing when he first got to KC?"

A fourth fan loyal to Florida State paid little attention to the embarrassing play: "Norvell was fired, and change is coming. We're good."

However, a fifth fan suggested the firing of Mike Norvell played a part: "When you fire your head coach, you're not really expecting much out of the rest of the season."

And lastly, one final fan pointed out how absurd it was to criticise the Seminoles: "Boston College runs a weird play, then loses the game and somehow you think this is FSU hitting a new low?"

Fans of the Seminoles will be hoping that this trick play will be the last of the embarrassing moments for them this season.

#2748. Spurs use dominant third quarter to deliver beatdown to Blazers

Last season, the Spurs had the second-best record in the league on the second night of back-to-backs, and surely their youth played a role in that. Believe it or not, they're still young just a few months later, and they are now 3-0 on SEGABABA's this season after an absolute beatdown of the Portland Trail Blazers for their 8th straight win. Portland started the season hot but were coming off a loss to the Lakers last night, and while they may have been revenge-minded for their first-round loss in the playoffs, they were missing Ja Morant, Robert Williams and Shaedon Sharpe and were no match for a healthy Spurs squad with Victor Wembanyama playing the way he is.

However, before the blowout came, the Spurs would have to get through a sluggish first half borne of both poor shooting from both teams and a heavy whistle. After hitting 3-5 from three before the first timeout, including both of Wemby's attempts for an 11-3 lead, both teams were sluggish, with the Spurs up shooting 33% in the quarter and the Blazers just 25%. But Portland got hot to close the quarter while the Spurs got sloppy, closing on a 7-0 run to cut the lead to two, 22-20.

After barely playing last night, Carter Bryant brought a spark to the start the second quarter with a couple of corner threes and a block of Damian Lillard. Meanwhile, the Blazers did a good job of drawing fouls and were in the bonus less than four minutes in. It didn't take long for the Spurs to join them, and what was already a sluggish game came to a screeching halt with all the whistles and free throws. Overall, the teams combined for 41 free throws in the half, and at one point, the Spurs scored 11 straight points from the stripe before a Stephon Castle alley-oop and consecutive Junliam Chamapgnie threes in the final minutes got the offense going again, and they went into the half up 64-49.

The lack of whistles allowed the offenses to open up in the second half, but the Spurs were red hot, especially Wemby, who finished the night with 29 points on 9-13 shooting (3-6 from three) in just 24 minutes of play. An 11-0 run capped off by a technical foul on Deni Avdija gave the Spurs their first 20-point lead of the game, and there was no stopping them from there. The Blazers had nothing left in the tank, and the crowd watched in stunned silence as the Spurs got the lead all the way up to 30 for the first time this season on a Dylan Harper banker late in the third quarter. The last 15+ minutes of the game was entirely garbage time, and the Spurs finished their most dominant game of the season with a 125-103 win.

We finally got a glimpse of last season's version of Luke Kornet. He was active in his first stint with a floater, two rebounds and block of a Chris Youngblood three-point shot, and the Spurs added a point to the lead. Granted, most of his time was spent against Yang Hansen, but he needed a confidence-booster, and maybe this was it. He finished the night with 6 points and 4 rebounds in 15 minutes, and perhaps most notably, was a +9 while on the floor.

As frustrating as all the whistles were for both sides in the first half, it was comical at times (granted it's easier to laugh when your team is ahead). Some of the calls were mindbogglingly soft, and Wemby former Spurs teammate Sidy Cissoko got into a bit of a French Flop Fest, with both exaggerating contact to get whistles. To borrow a hilarious text from Jesus Gomez last night, "Sidy flopped three times, and Wemby said, 'Hold my cabernet sauvignon'". (He also shook the refs' hands after the game, which I've never seen before, adding to the hilarity.)

Random thought of the night while sitting through a blowout: David Jones Garcia is still with the team instead of joining his fellow two-way players in Austin to start the season, which seems odd, but perhaps the Spurs intend to make him their 15th player once enough time has passed that they can sign him without going over the luxury tax, so he's staying with the main team? He really has nothing left to prove at the G League level, and he reportedly turned down more lucrative offers from overseas, so maybe there's an agreement in place? Just my two cents.

It wasn't the prettiest play of the game, but when trying to get out of the slugfest and free-throw-a-thon that was the second quarter, sometimes it just takes plays like this. (You also know it's your night when stuff like this goes in.)

The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. The timing is far from ideal. Bayern Munich will now have to navigate the coming weeks without its captain, its most experienced goalkeeper, and one of the most influential figures in the dressing room.

Three points against Mainz, but losing Neuer for potentially two months is a very steep price to pay. However, Urbig has been excellent this season and is rated by many to be the goalkeeper of the future for both Bayern Munich and Germany. #2742. Tyler Kolek owns up to Taylor Swift fan comment that earned him some fun Knicks ribbing

CLEVELAND — The visitors locker room sounded like a Sweet 16.

The setlist opened with "Shake It Off," followed by "You Belong With Me," "Style" and "Bad Blood."

The Knicks — led by DJ Jalen Brunson — were partying like it was "1989."

Tyler Kolek — who this week questioned Taylor Swift's Knicks fandom during an NBA 2K League livestream — may never, ever, ever hear the end of it from Swifties, but the second-year guard was hoping to make amends with one of the world's biggest stars following the Knicks' 109-97 win over the Cavaliers.

Tyler Kolek (13) looks to make a play during the Knicks' 109-97 win over the Cavaliers on Nov. 7, 2026 at Rocket Arena in Cleveland. NBAE via Getty Images

Kolek had labeled Swift the fakest celebrity Knicks fan on the bandwagon during their title run, calling the musician "performative" after she attended Game 4 of the NBA Finals at Madison Square Garden.

"It's just a question that was asked for me, that maybe I answered in the wrong way. Take that on the chin," Kolek said Saturday night. "I love her music. We were just playing it five minutes ago, and I'm singing every word to every song. Nothing against her at all.

"People have been going back and sending me all this stuff about her coming to the games, and she was actually wearing a [No.] 13 jersey [of] Joakim Noah back in the day with Carmelo [Anthony]. That's on me. I wasn't up to date on my Taylor Swift Knicks fandom. So that's on me."

The previous day, the Knicks put out a statement in support of Swift, whose wedding to Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce was held at the Garden this summer.

Taylor Swift jokes with her friend before the Knicks win over the Spurs in Game 4 at Madison Square Garden. Jason Szenes for the New York Post

"Taylor Swift has been a Knicks fan for many years, has a long history with Madison Square Garden, and we are incredibly appreciative of her support of the organization," a Knicks spokesperson said.

The Knicks returned to Cleveland for the first time since the Eastern Conference finals, when Swift attended Game 3 at Rocket Arena with Kelce — an Ohio native — and was seen cheering for the Cavaliers.

When Kolek called out Swift in the video with teammate Deuce McBride, he acknowledged he was "going to get some hate from the Swifties."

Since then, his teammates have taken their shots too.

"For sure, they're playing Taylor Swift in the locker room," Kolek said. "We were at practice [Friday and] we were playing Taylor. I love her music. I probably know more songs than anybody else in the locker room. Just misspoken."

#2739. Game Recap: Suns’ defensive intensity proves decisive in 102-99 win against Rockets

Rick Flair drip go "Woo!" on a(n)… all- time great.

The Suns dig deep to pull out a 102-98 victory over the Houston Rockets to win the KD trade for the first time this year.

What a wonderful game. One that gives us a blueprint for how the Suns are going to make noise in the perennially competitive Western Conference. This was a statement win and the best the Suns have tallied far, early in the season.

After tonight, I see a real path forward for the Suns to meet Ishbia's lofty goals of a second-round playoff appearance. In a game that could have been derailed by social media distractions, the Suns dug deep after a horrific 22-3 run to close the half to pull out a clutch-time victory against, possibly, the best team in the Western Conference. How did the Suns right the ship and pull out a competitive win against a team that swept the season series last year? Energy. The Phoenix Suns season is officially a question of energy.

So much has been made about fit but after tonight, it becomes irrelevant. It's not about the points, or the rebounds, or even the minutes a player delivers for the Phoenix Suns that will determine the wins and losses. It's the energy they can provide. Energy that leads to turnovers under the basket after a miss. Energy that leads to locking down defensive rebounds that lead to transition opportunities for the plethora of scorers on the Suns roster. Energy from blocks that lead to points, or drawing offensive fouls that take points away. The Suns rode the energy in the first quarter only to be hit by a brown out in the second, and in the end they found a way to generate enough power to match the Rockets' energy plays blow for blow through a contested third and outlasting a desperate Sengun (who doesn't want it with KhOso) looking to salvage a forgettable night with a fourth-quarter push that was too little too late.

I don't know if there is any player I can target as standing out in game that needed a whole team to secure a win. The Suns had 5 players finish the night in double figures, including a surgical Luke Kennard who proved to be the a fusion of Royce and Grayson Allen in a flurry of points in limited minutes. Booker put up 24 points on 24 shots, and Jalen Green went 50% from the field on 7-of-14 shooting, with 8 assists. The decision-making is coming along. The Villain, under the spotlight after his online spat with KD, held the former Sun to limited shots in the first half, but couldn't keep him off the line, where he grabbed 10 points on 11 attempts and ended the night with a hollow 21 points.

KhOso tag-teamed Sengun all night, who remained quiet for 3 and 1/2 quarters before making a push in the final six minutes. He finished the night with 15 points on 5/16 shooting with a modest 6 rebounds and a -16 plus-minus. If you're looking for a reason the Suns won the game, look no further than Sengun's 1-7 shooting with 4 minutes left in the third quarter. While there were plenty of mistakes from the young center duo, KhOso took advantage of some key injuries to Capella and Adams, and did enough inside to give the Suns the opportunity to win the game tonight.

It was the best of times; it was the worst of times.

The Suns got Jalen Green going early, starting 4-of-4 in the opening minutes of the game. I believe this needs to be a focus, and I was happy to see Jalen experience some success early against his former team. I no longer want to hear that Jalen Green can't play next to Devin Booker, as he consistently made the right decision and his paint touches became a real difference-maker for stretches in this game.

The Suns continued their stretch of hot starts, finding the energy early in a run sparked by Oso pulling the chair on Sengun, leading to a turnover and lay-up for Jalen Green. An offensive goal-tend led to an Oso "jumper", then Dillon bodied Durant into a bad pass, leading to a scramble with Dunn causing and then creating a turnover, which led to a Dillon three-pointer and a Houston timeout with the Suns leading 17-11.

The Suns continue to press, and Brooks draws an offensive foul, then hits an iso turnaround. Green makes a steal that leads to a corner three from Ryan Dunn, who had himself another night, and Kennard opens up the last three minutes, by splitting the black see opening up an assist to Ryan Dunn. Brooks hits a bucket, and Khaman shows promising hands as he collects a pass off a cut to the basket for a dunk. Kennard hits a jumper and a three to end the first quarter with the Suns up 35-23.

In the Second quarter, the Suns continued to cook, scoring an early six points before the system glitched and a scoring brownout, which lasted the length of the second quarter, led to a 41-23 lead for the Suns, turning into a tied score of 47-47 going into halftime. Is what happened.

A string of negative energy plays compounded into outright disaster, sparked off by four straight turnovers from the Suns team and caused by a series of quick shots, poor decisions, and offensive rebounds that snowballed into a 22-3 run going into halftime. For so many teams, this could have been the end, the beginning of the end, but the Suns managed to secure some extra juice in a game that was clearly important to the two former Houston Rockets who are looking to prove their value against the team that recently cast them aside.

The third quarter opens up with a previously quiet Durant hitting a three-point bucket that is immediately answered by the Phoenix Suns star Devin Booker with a three-point bucket of his own. This is what I loved about this third quarter, where every Houston push was answered in kind by the Phoenix Suns.

The Suns' path to victory is their ability to bring more energy than the opposing team. It was clear as day in the first quarter when the Suns made all the plays and shots they needed to push to an early double-digit lead, and unfortunately even more clear in a starkly different second half where the Houston Rockets woke up and matched the Suns' energy, systematically dismantling the gains the Suns had made. Too often this has led to a power outage from the Phoenix Suns, but not tonight.

A miscommunication on a switch between Booker and Bridges gives up an open three. Open three-point shots lead to the Rockets taking a 57-53 lead with 8 minutes left in the third.

Then Brooks contests a KD drive, which leads to Miles Bridges getting to the free-throw line for two shots. Positive energy. Then Brooks fouls KD on a three-point shot, bad energy, which pushes the Rockets' lead to 61-55.

Brooks and Dunn force a steal after a missed foul shot. Energy. Khaman knocks a ball free, and Booker dives to the floor, leading to a jump ball where the Rockets are called for a foul. Energy. The Suns collect the rebound on a Sengun miss, which turns into a Jalen Green dunk. Energy.

A Dillon Brooks hits a three, and a Durant miss leads to Booker heading to the foul line to regain the lead at 66-65. Energy. Kevin Durant hits a three, which is answered with a three from Devin Booker, with 2:25 left in the quarter. Energy. Dunn grabs an offensive rebound that led to a Collin Gillespie three-pointer. Energy. Durant gets an offensive rebound, and the Rockets are up 73-72. Negative energy.

Booker answers with a back door cut that leads to an easy bucket and the Suns regaining the lead 74-73.

Booker gets out in transition and earns a trip to the free-throw line. The Rockets win a challenge, and the Suns give up a straight drive to the basket to Fred, but Collin immediately answers with his own drive to the hoop. Energy. The Suns finish the third quarter up 76-75.

The fourth quarter opens up with Jalen Green attacking the paint. An early drive leads to a ManMan offensive rebound and putback. Khaman takes a trip to the free-throw line, and JG follows up with a jumper to push the Suns' lead to 80-75 . The Suns give up an offensive rebound to Smith, and Gillespie takes a bad shot, which leads to a Sheppard three and the Rockets tie the game up at 82-82.

Jalen Green contests a rebound that deflects out of bounds, and the Suns win a challenge to keep the ball on their end. A JG paint touch leads to a Malauch offensive rebound and one opportunity. Another Green paint touch leads to Bridges getting a mismatch and scoring in isolation.

Sengun and Miles Bridges exchange buckets. Sengun hits a three, but Dillon the Villain answers with a three of his own. Energy. Green gets into the paint and finds his way to the free-throw line where he hits 1-2 to give the Suns a 93-91 advantage.

Oso attempts an entry pass to a cutting Green, which gets fumbled out of bounds. Sengun takes it to the hoop to tie it up at 93-93. A Durant miss leads to a Booker middy, but Sengun fights his way to the foul line, hitting two foul shots to tie it back up at 95-95.

After a Durant miss, the Suns find Booker for an open three off an inbound, which he hits to take a 100-95 lead with 3 minutes left in the game. KD misses a shot on a Brooks contest, and Booker gets to the hoop for a lay-up to push the lead to 102-95. (Headband Book 4 L)

The Rockets bring it back to 102-97 when they turn it over on an attempted entry pass to a Sengun with 1:32 seconds left. Booker misses two straight shots, and Durant hits a jumper with 45 seconds left to bring the score to 102-99. Booker and Green work the two-man game, which leads to an out-of-bounds play and an in-and-out three from Booker with 3.2 seconds on the shot clock.

The Rockets have the ball within one score of tying it up, but the shot misses, and Oso collects the Rebound to secure a Suns' win in a season-altering momentum game.

The Phoenix Suns take on the San Antonio Spurs and their otherworldly seven-footer coming off a 50-point performance. Definitely an outsized task for a Suns team just starting to find their rhythm. Can the Suns continue to stack energy plays that lead to runs and secure a second straight win over a Western Conference contender? I hope so. Now that they've finally found their footing, they can't afford to slide back.

#2737. 5 questions with Mile High Report

The Denver Broncos are coming to Charlotte today with a slim hope of exceeding the 11 sacks that the Carolina Panthers have surrendered in the past two weeks. To figure out how slim that chance was—or not—and if Sean Payton has already worn out his welcome in Denver, I spoke with Laurie Lattimore-Volkmann over at Mile High Report. Here's what she had to say about that, Bo Nix's struggles, and more.

Bo Nix has not been having the season that many in Broncos country have been hoping for. What has held him back and how will he look to step his game up against the Panthers?

A lot has been made of Bo's offseason ankle surgery/recovery for his slow start to the season. I won't discount that that has likely played a role, despite him and the coaches saying he was feeling "just as mobile" at the beginning of the season as he had before the injury. Anyone who has competed in sports knows there is a mental hurdle to get past when coming back from an injury. But my guess is that it was a combination of many things, beginning with a little hesitation leftover from the injury, learning new terminology when Davis Webb did the play-calling, and playing the first six games against at least five of the top defenses in the league. A much smaller factor, but still one I believe impacted his play, is that Bo became a new dad this summer. Anyone who has kids and can remember that first year knows that you don't get anywhere near enough sleep. Some may laugh at that reason, but I believe it's impacted him a little. Watching Bo at the press conferences, it's clear he is exhausted and has zero f**** to give any naysayers. That's what being a new parent does to you!

Sean Payton is not a name that is greeted with respect or warmth in the Carolinas. How has his reception been so far in Denver?

A winning coach is always welcomed with open arms. Payton probably had to win over a few fans initially, but given the sh*tshow that preceded him, it didn't take much. He runs a tight ship, has great vision for the short and long-term plan for the team and has produced a winning product every season. And given that the rookie QB he chose to lead the team has worked out well, it means Payton is quite popular here.

The story of the season so far for the Carolina Panthers so far has been injuries. The most impactful have been along their offensive line. Does Denver try to generate pressure from the edge, the interior, from blitzing, or all of the above?

Panthers fans would like to know which weakness to be most afraid of on Sunday. Unfortunately for Bryce Young, there's not much of a weakness for your depleted O-line to take advantage of. Vance Joseph is phenomenal at disguising looks and bringing pressure – which is a dangerous combo. He doesn't blitz a ton, but it's generally effective when he does. Zach Allen and Malcolm Roach will generate a lot of pressure up the middle, allowing Nik Bonitto and Jonathan Cooper a good chance at the QB. And even when they don't get the sack, they can still rattle the quarterback enough to cause trouble for your offense. The defensive weakness to exploit is the linebackers, who are good tacklers but not particularly fast, as well as a slew of backup corners. But to do that, Young has to get to the receivers first.

Similarly, the secondary has been gutted by injuries, with three of their top four corners already on injured reserve and the fourth having yet to participate in practice this week. That has allowed the Panthers to surrender some historic rushing totals. Have Denver's rushing struggles this season come from trouble with their offensive line or from their running backs not being able to break tackles in the secondary?

That is a great question and if you can figure it out, Broncos Country would be thrilled. Every offseason we buy the hype that our running backs will finally be the group to take our run game to the next level. And every season, it seems like we spend a lot of energy in post-game commentary wondering where the run game is. I believe the play-calling/scheme is the main culprit. But we also haven't put a ton of draft or free agent capital into the position, so there is usually a lower ceiling with our RB room than we'd like to admit (which is why early rumors of Jonathan Taylor being traded to Denver had a lot of fans salivating). But there is a lot of hope for rookie Jonah Coleman and even second-year back RJ Harvey if he/they can stay healthy. If only Payton and Webb can commit to the run and create effective plays for it, there might be a chance.

At 6-2, the Broncos are riding pretty high at the moment. How confident are their fans in a win in Charlotte? Do you have a score prediction?

I think most fans are highly confident but also not immune to the fear of a trap game and/or the reality of how Broncos tend to play East Coast games (they haven't played particularly well in the 1 p.m. EST slot)! But as long as the Broncos don't beat themselves in the first half, I think the odds of a win are quite good. I'll go with Denver 28, Carolina 17.

#2734. Mikel Brown’s healthy but knows ‘it’s all about getting stronger’ for Nets

ATLANTA — Understand that "back" is the worst four-letter word for Nets fans.

They read about back woes, minutes limits and injury management, but Ben Simmons is what they see. And what they fear.

But with Mikel Brown Jr., they don't have to be afraid.

Despite the kid gloves the Nets have treated their rookie with, Brown's ankle is fine. And more importantly, so is his back.

Mikel Brown Jr., who scored 18 points, drives to the basket during the Nets' 124-121 loss to the Hawks on Nov. 7, 2026 in Atlanta. NBAE via Getty Images

While Brown was limited to 21 games for Louisville last season, sources told The Post that his back was structurally fine. That injury had just been a soft tissue one and is long since in the past. His current minutes limit is about the future and building strength for that — for who the Nets see as an eventual All-Star.

"It's all about getting stronger," Brown told The Post before scoring 18 points in the Nets' 124-121 loss to the Hawks on Saturday night. "This is my first year playing against this type of high level of athletes. You've got to be at an elite performance level body-wise. But that's just the everyday process when it comes to that stuff.

"I'm constantly in the weight room every day just strengthening the parts of my body I need to strengthen. But yeah, that's us going along with the plan. I'm all aboard with it. As long as we're winning games, that's all I care about."

With Brown being the reward for a long tanking season, fans are not only invested in his progress but still scarred from the Simmons experience — trading James Harden for what turned out to be just 90 ineffective games in three seasons.

"Nah, man, that was never the case," said Brown, who will not play Sunday in Dallas because he's not cleared for back-to-backs. "I've just been leaning on my performance staff. My body feels great. Just take it slow. It's an 82-game season. We want to be in a position to make the playoffs, so every game matters, but they're just like, 'the long run, the long run.' So taking it a game at a time, a day at a time, and attacking it. Everything's fine. I don't look at (social) media like that, but yes, everything's fine. My body's great, just continuing to build."

Brown has yet to play both legs of a back to back, with the Nets to play Sunday in Dallas.

Mikel Brown Jr. looks to shoot over Zuby Ejiofor during the Nets' road loss to the Hawks. AP

He entered Saturday averaging 12 points and four assists. And the game is visibly slowing down for the rookie, mustering 14.5 points in his last four tilts.

"I'm very happy with Mikel. Him in pick-and-roll, how fast he is, how shifty, he can shoot the 3, get to the rim. Very happy with his performance," coach Jordi Fernández said.

"It's always about playing hard, but it's also about playing smarter as well. So, just really having the game slow down," Brown told The Post. "I watched a lot of film with my coaches, a whole lot of film for myself, just slowing down and letting the game come to me and just letting the game flow.

"And just staying aggressive, living with the consequences if I turn the ball over, miss an assignment on defense, just knowing I have to get it back the next play. Just always having that next-play mentality. That's the mindset that's been in my head these past couple games."

Brown has particularly excelled in the pick-and-roll, capped by an 18 point, four-assist outing in their win over Charlotte. He shot 6 of 11, 3 of 5 from deep and had a highlight no-look pass to Moritz Wagner off a baseline drive.

"Yeah, really the willingness to just be myself and create plays within that pick-and-roll situation, whether that's hitting the pocket, reading the tag man. Just allowing the game to come to me. It's nothing I haven't worked on for freaking years before this. So I adapt and put it on show," Brown said.

"Great player. Big-time offensive spark," said Terance Mann. "He's gonna be good when he gets older, stronger, understands the game, understands the pick-and-roll situations. I could see him being an All-Star easily. He has a great basketball mind. So, it's fun to play with him."

The Nets are strengthening Brown's body, especially his core, searching for that All-Star outcome.
